extracted.intended_audience: artists, artisans, natural philosophers, physicians, and teachers (early modern learned readers)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for (1) recognizing natural signs and prodigies (pestilence, weather omens) and (2) methods, standards, and technical criteria for the arts (painting, sculpture, mechanical invention) and for teaching/writing those arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-pulverulence as a sign of pestilence
rubrics_metrics.description: If the air is as if powdered (puluerulentus) and retains this condition for several months, it foretells a pestilence of a certain kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes that impure, dust-laden air particularly injures the brain and that persistent dusty air over months signals a coming pestilence; this sign is presented as diagnostic alongside other signs (trees burning, animals affected).

rubrics_metrics.name: Trees burning as a certain omen of calamity
rubrics_metrics.description: If trees appear to burn (arbores ardere), this is a more certain sign of impending calamity than many other portents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author states that if trees burn it is a surer sign because it indicates the air itself is corrupted; this is presented as stronger evidence than some other signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals and fishes displaced by storms indicate prodigies/disease
rubrics_metrics.description: Eggs, young animals, frogs, fishes and other creatures carried and deposited by winds and storms into regions where they do not belong are reported as prodigies and possible signs of disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: ova parvorum animaliúm, ranarum & piscum transferred in gusts and storms; such transfers are often recorded after violent weather and considered portentous—use as part of a cluster of signs rather than singly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unusual avian deaths or birds found in trees as sign of severe pestilence
rubrics_metrics.description: Birds found dead in trees, or birds affected by disease, are taken as a great sign of coming pestilence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites reports (e.g., Joachim Schylerus) that during grave British pestilence birds were found dead in trees with pustules under their wings; such occurrences are classed among serious omens of epidemic disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rabies in dogs and wolves as indication of pestilential corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent rabies among dogs (and incursions of wolves) in or near towns is considered a sign of pestilence; these animals' madness indicates corrupted humours transmissible to humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text links rabid behavior of dogs and wolves to polluted waters or air; frequent rabies is considered an omen because the same causes that provoke rabies in animals can corrupt human humours and presage epidemic disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sheep afflicted before humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Sheep often suffer first in such seasons and thus their affliction is a sign for humans because their natures are more delicate and similar in certain humoral respects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author remarks that sheep (oves) are especially affected earlier than humans; observing livestock health is therefore diagnostic for impending human epidemics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proliferation of vermin in houses/walls indicates humid corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Great numbers of fleas, cockroaches (blattarum), worms, serpents and other creeping things appearing in dwellings and walls indicate excessive moisture and putrefactive vapors that are injurious and portend disease.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanation: the vermin are attracted by humid vapours rising from under the earth and from bedding; their abundance signals environmental conditions unfavourable to human health and may presage pestilence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bread that acquires mould overnight is an indication of pestilence
rubrics_metrics.description: If bread exposed to the air draws mould (mucorem) overnight, that is a sign that the air is already corrupt and may foretell pestilence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The passage links rapid corruption of bread to corrupt air; this is presented as one of the signs by which observers may infer the likely character of impending disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vermin/larvae in fruits and quick appearance of certain insects indicate fertility or sterility
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of worms, spiders, or flies in particular contexts is read as signs of fecundity or sterility depending on the creature: a fly born of humid, well-digested matter signals fertility; abundant spiders indicate sterility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: fly = fertile (humide tenue & bene concoctum); spider = cold and dry signifying sterility (aranea animal frigidum atque siccum). These diagnostic rules link micro-observations to agricultural or generative forecasts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divination taxonomy (fourfold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divination about the future is classed fourfold: (1) from unusual signs (portents), (2) from vapours and cloud-forms (vapours/nubium shapes), (3) from arts akin to natural skill (astrology, physiognomy, chiromancy, dream-interpretation, etc.), and (4) from prodigies, omens and auguries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises that these categories are varied and uncertain; while some observations are useful, many omens are ambiguous and require cautious, learned judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution in relying on omens — prefer learned observers
rubrics_metrics.description: Because signs and omens vary so much and are uncertain, it is neither decorous to observe them indiscriminately nor entirely safe to neglect them; a few learned persons should make judgments and keep to tested observations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text suggests selecting a small number of expert observers (the author says he would choose twelve) whose judgments are trusted rather than letting popular fancy run wild.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for teaching/writing an art or doctrine (division into species)
rubrics_metrics.description: To teach a doctrine perfectly, divide the subject into species and then subdivide those species repeatedly until reaching the smallest elements; demonstrate in both general doctrines and their affects, keeping genera and members properly contained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The instruction: separate the subject into species, then divide those into lesser ones until the last are reached; demonstrate both the doctrines and the affects that can be shown; do not treat too many genera at once; ensure that described members are contained under the treated genus.

rubrics_metrics.name: When demonstrating, limit scope and keep descriptions coherent
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid trying to cover too many kinds or genera in one treatment; each treated genus should include and contain the members described; failing this leads to uncertainty and wandering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This follows the teaching method advice: keep the division bounded by the art’s end, so the exposition remains clear and not vague or diffuse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for excellence among inventors and authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Greatness is judged by multiple qualities: subtlety (subtilitas), inventive novelty, practical utility, firmness and clarity of demonstration, arrangement and order of exposition, and the range of accomplishments (breadth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author exemplifies different virtues in different men (Archimedes for invention, Euclid for dogmatic firmness and perfect arrangement, Aristotle for dialectic and natural philosophy, Galen for medicine). Use these attributes when appraising technical authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtlety (subtilitas) as a high artistic virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtlety—the capacity for ingenious, delicate, and refined invention or argumentation—is repeatedly praised as a primary excellence in many arts (mechanics, mathematics, rhetoric, medicine, sculpture, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns that subtility can take many forms and that multiple kinds of subtility are laudable; it underpins success in technical arts and is often what distinguishes outstanding works or inventors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Painting’s three essential parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Painting comprises three parts: delineation (drawing/outline), the work of the hand (making/relief), and color (including light and shadow / umbrae).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author says that painting demands delineation, color, and chiaroscuro: in plane (tabula) one must supplement with shadows and delineations; white in particular affects perception (making small letters appear smaller) and the use of shadows/obscurity aids deception and illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for representing temporal succession and 'fading' in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: To show successive processes or temporal succession in painting, use layering and dilution of colors: earlier stages should be represented paler or more obsolete than later ones; administrators of the example: the latrunculi game where successive moves are shown by altering color intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detailed example: in a sequence of figures, the first process (earliest) should be paler/diluted/obsoleted to suggest prior action, middle steps more distinct, and final stage most vivid. Use of position, color dilution and shadow achieves the temporal illusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on depicting faces/portraits
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole face is harder to represent than the middle (half) face; begin by conceiving the whole via an imagined middle symmetry, since the middle provides more recognizable lines, wrinkles and features than a lateral half.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice: conceive the whole in memory and mark a central sketch; the middle face allows a better, more complete representation because more diagnostic features are visible; dimidiated (half) faces are easier for recognition but less exquisitely representational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative difficulty of arts and scales
rubrics_metrics.description: Different arts and different scales have distinct difficulties: the plastic arts (modeling/sculpture) are the purest and most difficult overall; both very large and very small works have special difficulties while medium-sized works are often easier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: sculpture's fine delicacies, engraving/celare's special difficulty (conceiving carved-out forms), and that minor works may require extraordinary subtlety while medium works are more manageable; the author emphasizes that scale influences technique and difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engraving/‘celare’ vs sculpture — conceiving hollow forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Engraving or making incised (celare) images (e.g., on gems) is often harder than sculpting protruding forms, because the engraver must envision the recessed space and cannot see the final effect until completed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explains practical problems: when carving a cavity, any mis-addition or mis-removal is hard to remedy; the cognitive task of simultaneously conceiving the hidden interior form makes engraving especially demanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and evaluation of mechanical inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanical inventions are to be admired both for subtlety and practical effectiveness; novel devices (clockwork without rope, toothed wheels, arrangements for stable seats on moving chariots, large glass spheres representing the heavens) are praised as signs of genius when they are feasible and demonstrably functional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text enumerates mechanical contrivances (toothed wheels, clockworks, armillary-like machines) and suggests that such machines should be judged by ingenuity, functionality and the ability to represent complex motions; feasibility and demonstrable operation are critical to their evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of optical and material tricks in painting
rubrics_metrics.description: Painters should employ optical knowledge and material artifices (color mixing, white pigment, shadowing, varnishes/pastes) to create illusions and to adjust apparent sizes and distances; these tricks contribute vitally to the success of pictorial deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: addition of white to alter perception; use of darkness and architectural framing to deceive the eye; use of layered varnishes (papieri) and glazes to make painted images appear real; painters must know mechanics of vision to deceive the senses effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance admiration for ancient and modern inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Although antiquity produced many admirable works, modern times also produce new inventions and should not be disparaged; inventions should be judged on their merits rather than age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author defends contemporary inventors and lists numerous recent devices and refinements, advising readers to both admire ancient achievements and recognize modern ingenuity and utility.
